newsitem.title: USA: North Dakota newspaper survives flood, fire.
newsitem.headline: North Dakota newspaper survives flood, fire.

text.p: The Grand Forks Herald, evicted from its home by fire and flood, hit newspaper stands on Tuesday a few hours late, but welcomed by readers willing to forgive the delay.

Despite its troubles, the Herald's staff has kept the paper up and running. The paper that hit stands Tuesday was airlifted in from the presses of the St. Paul Pioneer Press, a fellow Knight-Ridder publication in Minnesota.
"It took us about 30 seconds on Saturday morning to decide that we were going to have a Sunday newspaper," said Jim Durkin, newroom manager at the Herald.
Like many of residents of this disaster zone, the Herald was evacuated from its home last weekend. Floodwaters from the Red River forced the paper to leave its offices in downtown Grand Forks.
Then the paper lost its newsroom and its circulation department to a devastating fire that ripped through a dozen downtown buildings.
Some media reports have called it "the little paper that could," and President Clinton openly expressed amazement at its tenacity.
"How in the world they kept producing a newspaper for you is beyond me," Clinton told a cheering crowd of evacuees Tuesday at the Air Force Base 15 miles west of Grand Forks.

The Herald found a temporary home Saturday in a computer lab at the University of North Dakota. Journalists wrote articles and then beamed them electronically to the Pioneer Press, where they found their way onto newsprint.
But just when the Herald was settling in to its new digs, it had to leave when the campus came under mandatory evacuation orders because of the spreading flood.
The paper was adopted Sunday by the Manvel Elementary School, an orange-brick building with 205 students and 15 teachers that sits about 10 miles north of Grand Forks.
Principal Richard Ray said the decision to invite the Herald to stay until the end of summer was just the school's way of helping local relief efforts.
"We just though that the local newspaper is important to our people. It has to be published and we had the facility," Ray said.
"A second reason is this is a teachable moment for our kids. They're learning about sharing and community, and this is what you do to help people out."

Reporters worked in a stuffy classroom filled with Apple Macintoshes and photographers process their pictures down the hallway. Students, meanwhile, adjusted to the hubbub that has overtaken their school.

Knight-Ridder CEO Tony Ridder reassured staff Tuesday that the company will rebuild the Herald offices, but some things have been lost forever. The fire gutted all of the Herald's microfiche, including copies of the original paper.
"We lost our whole library -- all our negatives. We have no history," Durkin said.
Erin Campbell, an agriculture reporter at the Herald, hinted that some losses were more personal.
"My favourite photo of my father and I," she said when asked what she lost. "He passed away a year and a half ago."
